title: Natural Deduction
body:
**Natural deduction** derives a conclusion from premises by applying inference rules, one line
at a time, each justified by a rule and the lines it was applied to. The finished sequence is a
proof.

```
Show R, given P → Q, Q → R, and P.

1. P → Q          premise
2. Q → R          premise
3. P              premise
4. Q              1, 3  modus ponens
5. R              2, 4  modus ponens
```

Each line is either a premise, an assumption, or the result of a rule, and the justification
column is what makes the proof checkable by somebody who did not write it.

The core rules are [[Modus Ponens]], [[Modus Tollens]] and the
[[Hypothetical Syllogism]], alongside introduction and elimination rules for each
connective. Two rules discharge an assumption. Conditional proof assumes the antecedent,
derives the consequent, and concludes the conditional. Indirect proof assumes the negation of
the goal, derives a contradiction, and concludes the goal, which is
[[Proof By Contradiction]] as a formal rule.

Compared with a [[Truth Table]], a derivation scales with the difficulty of the argument
while a table scales with the number of letters, so a derivation handles arguments no table
could fit. Its weakness is the other side of the same property: failing to find a proof
establishes nothing, because the failure might be yours. Proving an argument invalid needs a
[[Counter-Model]].
